Julien has invited Ioana to a big concert at the Lyon Opera. Ioana needs a dress. She goes with Sophie, the baker, to a shop on Rue Victor-Hugo.
Hello, ladies. Can I help you?
Yes, I’m looking for a dress for a concert.
What colour? We have lovely black, red, blue dresses…
Look at this green dress, Ioana! It’s beautiful, isn’t it?
Yes, it’s very pretty. Can I try it on?
Of course. What size are you?
A 38, I think. In Romania it’s the same size.
Here you are. The fitting room is at the back, on the right.
(She comes out of the fitting room.) Well? It’s a bit small, isn’t it?
A bit, yes. Do you have the next size up?
Yes, here’s the 40. This style is very elegant.
Perfect, this one fits me well! How much is it?
Ninety euros. But today there’s a sale: thirty per cent off!
Sixty-three euros! That’s a bargain. And these black shoes to go with it?
No, no! I don’t need new shoes. I’ll just take the dress. Can I pay by card?
you do (“faire du 38” = to wear a size 38)
goes (“aller bien” = to suit, to fit)
With many adjectives you hear the difference: vert = “vehr”, verte = “vehrt”; petit = “puh-TEE”, petite = “puh-TEET”. With “bleu / bleue” or “noir / noire” there’s no audible difference.
Beau = “bo”, belle = “bel”. Nouveau = “noo-VO”, nouvelle = “noo-VEL”. The forms are completely different.
Ce = “suh” (weak e), ces = “say” (closed e), cette = “set”. Careful: “ces” and “ses” (his/her) sound the same.
AIL is read “eye”: travail = “tra-VYE”. EUIL = “uhy”: fauteuil = “fo-TUHY”. And “taille” = “tye”.
Je peux, tu peux, il peut all sound “puh”. Ils peuvent = “puhv”.
Unlike English, French adjectives agree with the noun in gender and number. Basic rule: feminine = +e, plural = +s.
already end in -e: stay the same
“Marron” (brown) and “orange” never change: des chaussures marron, une veste orange. They come from the names of fruit (chestnut, orange).
Unlike English, most French adjectives come AFTER the noun: une robe rouge (a red dress), un film intéressant, un livre français.
But a few short, very common adjectives come BEFORE. You can spot them with the BAGS rule: Beauty, Age, Goodness, Size:
Before a plural adjective, “des” becomes “de”: “des robes” → “de jolies robes”. That’s what the shop assistant says in the dialogue.
“Beau”, “nouveau” and “vieux” have a special form before a masculine noun starting with a vowel: un bel appartement, un nouvel ami, un vieil homme.
English distinguishes “this” and “that”. French doesn’t: “ce manteau” can mean “this coat” or “that coat”. To be precise you add -ci (here) or -là (there): ce manteau-ci, ce manteau-là.
The pronouns (without a noun) are: celui-ci (this one), celle-ci (this one, feminine), ceux-ci, celles-ci. Ioana says: “Celle-ci me va bien” (This one fits me well).
4. The verb POUVOIR = can, to be able to
After “pouvoir” comes an infinitive, just like English “can” + verb:
“Vouloir” (chapter 5) and “pouvoir” are conjugated almost the same way: je veux / je peux, ils veulent / ils peuvent.
Je peux vous aider ? — Non merci, je regarde.
Vous faites quelle taille ? — Du 38. (shoes: Je fais du 39)
Vous avez la taille au-dessus / en dessous ?
Elle me va bien. / Elle est trop grande, trop petite.
Je la prends. / Je vais réfléchir.
Je peux payer par carte ? / en espèces ?
“Les soldes” are the big sales in January and July, with dates set by law in France. “Une bonne affaire” = a bargain.
Prices: “vingt-neuf euros quatre-vingt-dix-neuf” (29,99 €). French uses a comma for decimals, not a point.
Can I try these trousers on?

Karim has a problem: next Saturday he’s going to his cousin Mehdi’s wedding in Marseille. And he doesn’t have a suit.
He has an old grey suit, but it’s too small. “I can’t wear that! It’s the suit from my own wedding, ten years ago!”
So on Wednesday afternoon Karim goes to a department store with Ioana. Ioana has good taste, says his wife Leïla.
The shop assistant is very elegant. He’s wearing a pink shirt and a purple tie. “Hello, sir. Can I help you?”
“I’m looking for a suit for a wedding. Not too expensive, please.”
The assistant shows him a black suit. Karim tries it on. “It’s too serious. I’m not going to a funeral!”
Next, a light blue suit. Ioana laughs: “In that suit you look like a sailor!”
Finally the assistant brings a beautiful navy-blue jacket and grey trousers. Karim comes out of the fitting room. Ioana and the assistant say together: “Perfect!”
“How much is it?” asks Karim. “Two hundred and forty euros for the jacket and the trousers.”
Karim pulls a face. It’s expensive… But he looks in the mirror. He looks handsome. Really handsome.
“I’ll take them. And this purple tie too!”
In the evening Leïla looks at the tie and says nothing. Then she smiles: “Well… for a wedding in Marseille, it’s perfect.”
ago (with time: “il y a dix ans” = ten years ago)
